messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir, a 40-year-old paramedic, still remembers the smell of the hospital antiseptic that night. He had been on duty when the call came in—a motorcycle accident, high speed, multiple trauma. He recognized the jacket before he saw the face. It was his younger brother, Samir. The visible injuries were catastrophic, and despite Amir’s frantic efforts, Samir died on the gurney. In the months that followed, Amir found that certain moments would send him spiraling: the sight of any visible wound on a patient, the sudden antiseptic scent that hit him when walking into the ER, or even a passing mention of accident victims. Each of these triggers would yank him back into that full-sensory reliving—the sound of the sirens, the warmth of blood on his gloves, the crushing weight of his own helplessness. There were whole stretches of the event he could not retrieve, no matter how hard he tried, and that gap felt like proof that his mind had simply shut down when it mattered most.

The memory brought back the same terror, and Amir came to believe he had permanently changed for the worse. Because the memory returned with such visceral force, he began to see reminders of it everywhere — in the colour of a patient's jacket, in the sound of a distant siren, in the way a colleague's hands moved. He told himself he should have protected Samir, that he couldn’t rely on himself anymore. These negative appraisals gnawed at him constantly: every time a new shift began, he felt his failure pressing on his chest. The trauma, he was certain, had broken something essential in him. That belief made him more watchful, more inclined to scan rooms for danger, and he began choosing where to sit based on how protected he felt—always with his back to a wall, facing the door. His concentration faltered; he would lose his train of thought mid-sentence when a colleague’s hand brushed his shoulder, making him startle with alarm. Living in this state of constant alert, Amir had come to see his hypervigilance as the most damning evidence that the trauma had shattered something permanent in him.

To cope, Amir developed a pattern of avoidance. He started calling in sick to work more often, staying home rather than exposing himself to the visual injuries and hospital smells that tormented him. Yet each place he avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way he drove to avoid the hospital's emergency bay was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened, etching the event deeper into his daily landscape. Yet when he did go in, he threw himself into overworking—taking every extra shift, staying late, running from one call to the next—keeping his mind so occupied that he didn’t have to think about the trauma. He tried hard to suppress the memories, but the more he pushed them away, the more they erupted unbidden. The suppression itself seemed to feed the memory gaps, and the terror on recall grew sharper each time. Overworking left him exhausted, and the exhaustion only reinforced his sense that he couldn’t rely on himself—that he was constantly running from something inside him.

The cycles interlocked. Triggers at work—a child with a bleeding laceration, the smell of disinfectant—would immediately spike his threat response, making him jumpy and hypervigilant for the rest of the shift. That heightened threat then pulled his mind back to the reliving, and the reliving deepened his conviction that he had failed. He began to interpret small things as signs that he would fail again: a pager going off, a glance from a supervisor. His negative appraisals fed the threat, and the threat made him more sensitive to triggers he might otherwise have ignored. The avoidance and overworking, meanwhile, kept him from ever processing the event; each time he suppressed a thought, the memory returned more vividly, and each memory reinforced his sense of permanent damage. Even his wife noticed he had become distant, pulling away from touch, always scanning the room during dinner. He couldn’t explain why he needed to sit with his back to the wall; it just felt necessary.

He finally came to therapy after his wife told him she couldn’t bear to see him so afraid. Amir admitted he was terrified that he would never be the man he used to be—that the trauma had left a wound that could not heal. He wanted to stop the cycle, but he didn’t know how.
